title: John 7:10–24
context: After his brothers go up, Jesus goes to the feast privately. Jerusalem mutters and fears. Mid-feast he teaches in the temple: his teaching is from the One who sent him; anyone whose will is to do God’s will will know the teaching’s origin. He exposes Sabbath hypocrisy over Moses’ circumcision and calls them to judge with right judgment, not appearances.

verses.text: But when his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly, but as it were in secret.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: this was his last journey but one to Jerusalem; the next time he went up he suffered. He does go—but not as they demanded, not in their caravan, not as a candidate.

Private going is still coming. The offer will be public in the temple; the approach refuses their stage-management. He keeps the feast without keeping their script.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin has already set him coming secretly until office requires an open stand. Private is not timid; it is timed. He will teach mid-feast in the teeth of armed dislike.

The Son’s itinerary is holy. He neither deserts the feast nor lets unbelief choreograph the entrance. When he appears, it will be as teacher, not as spectacle.

verses.text: The Jews therefore sought him at the feast, and said, “Where is he?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the Jews—the men of Judea, particularly of Jerusalem. “Where is he?” can be hunger or hunt. The feast feels his absence before it hears his voice.

Seeking can be honest or hostile. The question is already a kind of light: they know he belongs in the conversation. What they will do when he answers is still before them as responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the people gape for promised redemption like hungry men, yet when Christ appears they remain in suspense. “Where is he?” shows they knew the man and had not yet been earnestly moved; they stay in doubt.

Curiosity is not faith. A church can miss its own feast-guest and still mouth his name. The later teaching will divide this looking into muttering and, in some, the beginning of belief.

verses.text: There was much murmuring among the multitudes concerning him. Some said, “He is a good man.” Others said, “Not so, but he leads the multitude astray.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: much whispering among those from distant parts. The crowd splits into moral compliment and a charge of seduction—neither yet the confession of chapter 20.

Division here is the sound of a decision in process. “Good man” is too small; “leads astray” is slander. Grace has put enough of him before them that neutrality is already leaking. They may still come further—or harden the whisper into a verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: it is not a new evil that men differ about Christ even in the bosom of the Church. Rashness is great in the things of God; they hurry to judgment on the Son while they would be modest in small matters. Yet in a confused multitude some think aright, though swallowed by the bewildered many.

Dissension around the Word is not proof the Word is unclear. The marks and brands of Christ include being called an impostor. Remain faithful; do not let the split unsettle you into silence.

verses.text: Yet no one spoke openly of him for fear of the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: no one spoke openly in his favor, for fear of those in authority. The muttering stays in side rooms because the rulers have made his name expensive.

Fear is a pressure, not an excuse that erases duty. Some who whisper now will later speak; some will stay safe. The gospel still sincerely calls the frightened to open speech, without pretending the cost is light.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: by “the Jews” here, the rulers. They burned to bury his name in oblivion. Silence under fear is gross tyranny—a wretched condition when freedom is oppressed. Yet Christ’s power will shine brighter when he makes himself heard amidst armed foes.

Unbridled license is not the church; neither is terror. The Son will not wait for a free press. He teaches when the Father opens a mouth in a hostile temple.

verses.text: But when it was now the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple and taught.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: the feast lasted eight days; this was probably a Sabbath. He went up directly into the temple, without stopping elsewhere. Mid-feast, mid-crowd, he takes the teacher’s place.

Teaching is the form of the offer. He does not merely appear; he opens the Sender’s doctrine to whoever will hear. A public lesson in the temple is as wide as the courts will hold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he was not so afraid as to desist from office; delay was so that he might preach to a very large assembly. We may expose ourselves to dangers, but ought never to omit an opportunity of doing good. He teaches according to ancient custom: ceremonies without doctrine are cold spectacles.

The great High Priest undertakes the teacher’s office because priests were dumb and doctrine leavened. He attempts nothing but by the Father’s command.

verses.text: The Jews therefore marveled, saying, “How does this man know letters, having never been educated?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: how comes he to be so acquainted with sacred literature as to expound with propriety and gracefulness, seeing he has never learned at any place of education? Their marvel is half compliment, half dismissal.

They have light enough to see that the teaching is not homemade. Instead of kneeling, they file a credentials objection. Unbelief often sounds like an admissions office.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: those who think he is being honored are mistaken. The astonishment seeks occasion to despise him. If God uses ordinary means, the means veil his hand; if unwonted power shines, we are stunned and let it pass as a dream. They despise the grace because it exceeds their capacity.

Pride takes no interest in what it cannot diagram. Admonished by them, learn deeper reverence in considering God’s works.

verses.text: Jesus therefore answered them, “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: my doctrine is not mine—acquired by any labor of learning; but his that sent me—immediately infused by him. The scandal of no school is actually a ladder to the Sender.

He gives them a testable claim. The teaching can be known as God’s. He does not ask for blind personality-cult; he points away from himself-as-self to the Father, and still holds hearers responsible for what they now hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the circumstance that offended them was a ladder to perceive God’s glory. The Father determined that the Son should go out of a mechanic’s workshop rather than the schools of the scribes, that none might think the gospel fabricated on earth. Authority of spiritual doctrine is from God alone.

Every teacher must be able to refer doctrine to God as author and to a sending. What is merely ours may be despised; what the Father sends may not.

verses.text: If anyone desires to do his will, he will know about the teaching, whether it is from God or if I am speaking from myself.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: if any man be willing to do his will, he shall know of the doctrine—a universal rule for all persons and doctrines. He that is thoroughly willing to do it shall certainly know what the will of God is. Knowledge of origin follows a will that wants obedience, not a seminar that wants leverage.

The passage carries conditionality without Pelagius. Prevenient grace restores the capacity to be willing; the verse is a sincere address: will to do, and you will know. Remaining unsure is often unwillingness wearing the mask of intellectual caution. “Anyone” is not a trick word. The teaching can be resisted; the willing are not a closed caste.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: sound judgment flows from fear and reverence for God. Nothing else hinders us from judging aright but that we are unruly and headstrong. If we are prepared to obey, he will illuminate by the Spirit. These words define true religion: being prepared heartily to follow God’s will, which no man can do unless he has renounced his own views. They whose hearts are right will never be deceived.

The promise is earnest, and the willingness is not native. Unruly hearts do not elect themselves into piety. The Spirit who illuminates also makes the heart willing; those he so prepares do know. The verse is not a ladder of unaided will; it is Christ’s diagnosis of why they cannot see.
verses.keyContrast: Both refuse a merely academic test of Jesus’ teaching. Arminians typically take “if anyone desires to do his will” as a genuine, grace-enabled condition anyone may meet or resist. Reformed interpreters typically read the same words as a promise to the willing, while holding that no one is so willing unless God has already humbled and illumined the heart.

verses.text: He who speaks from himself seeks his own glory, but he who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and no unrighteousness is in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: there is no unrighteousness in him—no deceit or falsehood. Self-origin and self-glory travel together; the sent One aims at the Sender’s honor, and that is how you know the teaching is true.

Weigh teachers by whose name they burnish. Christ meets his own criterion in public. Hearers who still prefer a glory of their own will call even this honesty a threat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: everything that displays God’s glory is holy; everything that exalts men and obscures that glory ought to be rejected. He who aims at God’s glory will not go wrong; this is the touchstone. No man can faithfully teach unless void of ambition.

No falsehood is not a mood. It is the moral signature of a messenger who has nowhere to stand but the Father’s honor. Ambition in the pulpit is already a doctrinal crack.

verses.text: Didn’t Moses give you the law, and yet none of you keeps the law? Why do you seek to kill me?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: ye are unrighteous; ye violate the very law ye profess zeal for. The murder-plot is not Torah-faithfulness. Moses is on Jesus’ side against their selective zeal.

He still reasons with them. The law they boast of already condemns the intent to kill. They could repent of the plot; the question “why” is not rhetorical fatalism but a door.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: he tears the mask. They freely violate the law they claim to defend; therefore they are not moved by love of it. Drag the wicked from concealments when they fight the gospel under pious slogans.

Zeal for Moses without keeping Moses is already judgment. The law they wield will not justify the desire to kill the Lawgiver’s sent Son. Their rage has another source than holiness.

verses.text: The multitude answered, “You have a demon! Who seeks to kill you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: thou hast a devil—a lying spirit. These, coming from distant parts, probably did not know the priests’ design. Distance can be innocence; it can also be unbelief that treats a true warning as madness.

Not every hearer is in on the plot, but every hearer is responsible for the Speaker. Calling the warning demonic is easier than asking whether it is true. Grace still offers them a better hearing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: “thou art mad”—a Jewish idiom for rage or lost reason as diabolic torment. The multitude reproaches him with simplicity; the common people did not know the priests’ intent. Be cautious not to judge what you do not understand; if rashly condemned, digest the affront mildly.

Ignorance of a plot does not make the crowd a safe jury. They still have the teaching and the Speaker. Madness-language is how unbelief often names the truth that threatens it.

verses.text: Jesus answered them, “I did one work and you all marvel because of it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: I did—at the pool of Bethesda—one work out of many; and ye all marveled, amazed because I did it on the Sabbath. Sixteen months of anger, in his counting, sit on a healing.

They marvel at mercy as if it were the scandal. The work was good; the marvel is unbelief’s way of staring without repenting. He will now reason from Moses rather than merely assert power.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: leaving their persons, he speaks of the fact. He is blamed for a single work—the Sabbath cure—while they do many like works on every Sabbath in circumcision and do not count them criminal.

He will not let the marvel stay aesthetic. The work is God’s; their amazement is already a kind of judgment on their inconsistency. Truth will now compare the greater good with their lesser exception.

verses.text: Moses has given you circumcision (not that it is of Moses, but of the fathers), and on the Sabbath you circumcise a boy.
verses.arminianNotes:
Wesley: because Moses enjoined circumcision (though far more ancient) you think it no harm to circumcise on the Sabbath—and are angry at him for a greater good, healing a man body and soul on the Sabbath.

He honors both Moses and the fathers. Right judgment would rejoice that Sabbath already bends for covenant mercy. They could have used the same canon to welcome the healing; they prefer the appearance of rigor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: circumcision was enjoined so as to be necessary even on the Sabbath; thus it is demonstrated that Sabbath worship is not violated by the works of God. Moses, who rigidly demanded Sabbath-keeping, still commanded the eighth-day rite even when it fell on the day of Rest.

God’s works agree with God’s works. The exception they already practice is the principle they deny in him. Their canon is not too strict; it is selective.

verses.text: If a boy receives circumcision on the Sabbath, that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because I made a man completely healthy on the Sabbath?
verses.arminianNotes:
From a wound of covenant sign to a whole-body making-well: the comparison is from lesser to greater. If Sabbath may host circumcision so Moses is not broken, it may host the Messiah’s mercy without being broken.

Anger here is a decision. They are not forced by Torah to hate the healing. Willing to do God’s will (v. 17) would have recognized the greater good. The question still invites a better judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: both works are God’s; the cure is more excellent because its benefit extends to the whole man—body joined to spiritual advantage, not a mere bodily relief that would lose the comparison. They slander a work in which grace shines more illustriously than in the circumcision they honor.

The argument is not a loophole. It is a claim that the Son’s mercy is the Sabbath’s fulfillment, not its foe. Anger at that mercy is already a verdict on their seeing.

verses.text: Don’t judge according to appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Face, party, and Sabbath optics have been their court. Right judgment would have weighed the work by God’s intent, not by the embarrassment of an unauthorized healer.

The imperative assumes they can yet judge rightly. The call is sincere. Prevenient grace and the teaching now in their ears make a just verdict possible; remaining at appearances is not unfortunate dimness but refusal of the light they have.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: having finished the defense, he reproves them for being carried by wicked dispositions rather than by fact. Circumcision on the Sabbath did not violate the Law because God’s works agree. Why not conclude the same about Christ’s work, except that prejudice against his person has preoccupied them? Judgment will never be right unless regulated by the truth of the fact—especially about heavenly doctrine, which we are prone to dislike for hatred or contempt of the man.

Appearances include credentials, Galilee, and crowd. Right judgment begins when God is allowed to be God in the work, even when the Worker offends our party.
